extracted.intended_audience: journalism and media-literacy teachers (and students) who use NPR material in the classroom
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and classroom-ready criteria for determining whether a story is newsworthy and for teaching students to judge/produce newsworthy journalism. Includes traditional news values, examples of failures, and a two-part classroom assignment structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the audience in on why the work matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience members should be able to discern why a story is valuable to them. And when it's not obvious, the journalist needs to make it obvious by articulating the promise, either in the headline or early in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the value isn't clear, the journalist should state the journalistic purpose up front (headline or lead). Example: NPR's coverage of the Rich Lowry viral clip failed because it asked whether he said a slur and did not definitively answer, so it did not "bring any value to the audience."

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness
rubrics_metrics.description: The information or the developments are truly new, meaning they've come to light in recent days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should report recently revealed facts or developments; newness is a traditional news value that helps justify coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: The topic itself is of interest at this moment, meaning it's timely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story's relevance often depends on current events and public attention; timeliness can make an otherwise small item newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance/usefulness to the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: The story itself is relevant to the audience, meaning it is useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coverage should bring utility or actionable information to the audience — i.e., explain why the audience should care or how the information affects them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrigue (interesting people/companies/events)
rubrics_metrics.description: The people, companies or events are intriguing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A subject's intrinsic interest or notoriety can justify coverage; choose subjects with curiosity-driving characteristics or recognizable significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusualness / human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The events of a particular story are unusual; this is often called 'human interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories that reveal surprising, atypical, or emotionally resonant situations can be newsworthy even absent broader policy significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict or tension to be resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: There is conflict or tension to be resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News often centers on controversy, disagreement, or unfolding tension; coverage that helps explain or resolve that tension serves audience understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer central questions / provide reporting that brings value
rubrics_metrics.description: A story should not pose a central question and then fail to answer it; asking a question and then not answering it means the story doesn't bring value to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience cannot easily determine why a story is worth reading or listening to, reporters need to do additional reporting. The Lowry item is used as an anti-pattern — the piece raised whether he said a slur but did not resolve the question, so it lacked value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify prominence/airtime and explain why a source/guest matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists need to explain in the setup why an interview subject's views or a person's prominence merit coverage or airtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Morning Edition's interview with Gordon Sondland required more information in the introduction to clarify why listeners should spend seven minutes with him — reporters should explain a guest's relevance, history, or impact to justify focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide context, scope, and quantitative specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should give context about scale and representation (e.g., how many campuses experienced protests; what percentage of students participated) so audiences can judge significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid implying broad or universal significance when coverage is of a limited subset. Be explicit about numbers, proportions, and whether described events were isolated or widespread — this helps audiences accurately assess newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe the journalistic purpose in the body of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists should 'describe the journalistic purpose of their work out loud, in the body of the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making the reporting aim explicit (investigation, accountability, explaining a trend, representing a point of view) helps audiences understand why the piece was produced and how to evaluate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom lesson components: The Context, The Background, In the Field
rubrics_metrics.description: Each educator installment should address three themes: The Context (dives into the subject and why it's important in journalism), The Background (uses analysis and external resources to show how the issue plays out), and In the Field (gives students an opportunity to apply what they've learned, including a handout).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For teaching newsworthiness, provide context and significance, connect to prior analysis/resources (e.g., Poynter), and include an applied exercise/handout for students to practice judging or producing newsworthy coverage.
